The European grayling Thymallus thymallus exhibits several critical life-history traits that vary with thermal regime during early development. Embryonic development is particularly temperature-sensitive, with eggs incubated at 8 °C [T = 8 °C] requiring approximately 22 days  to hatch. In contrast, raising the incubation temperature to 13 °C [T = 13 °C] accelerates development considerably, reducing the age at hatch to about 14.7 days . At the warmest tested conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], hatching occurs most rapidly, occurring after just 8 days . Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae measure roughly 1.7 cm  in total length at hatch, a modest size that reflects the relatively small, demersal eggs characteristic of this salmonid. This initial length provides a baseline for evaluating subsequent growth trajectories under differing environmental conditions.

Reproductive investment in female grayling has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. At a sustained water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a value of approximately 16.7% [GSI = approximately 16.7%] prior to the spring spawning period. This index is consistent with the iteroparous strategy typical of many Thymallus populations, where females divide annual reproductive effort across multiple years. The dataset from which these values derive, referenced by IngrIbbo20aa, indicates that the species' reproductive thermal window spans from 3 °C to 11 °C, meaning the 7 °C [T = 7 °C] condition falls well within the natural range experienced by spawning adults in boreal rivers.

Body size thresholds mark important transitions in the grayling life cycle. The attainment of sexual maturity, for instance, is closely tied to a total length of approximately 23 cm [Lp = approximately 23 cm], a size that individuals typically reach after several growing seasons in temperate river systems. Once mature, females continue to grow toward an ultimate total length of about 60 cm [Li = about 60 cm], a value that represents the maximum size documented in well-established populations. Mature females at the upper end of this size range, specifically those reaching 45 cm in total length , exhibit a remarkably high reproductive output. At 7 °C [T = 7 °C], a female of this size, weighing approximately 1160 grams at an age of 9 years, produces roughly 99.3 eggs per day over the course of a single spawning season (approximately 99.3 eggs per day) .

Longevity and the timing of first reproduction are additional parameters that define the grayling's life-history strategy. Field records indicate that the oldest documented individuals reach a maximum lifespan of approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], a longevity that places Thymallus thymallus among the longer-lived European salmonids. First reproduction, however, occurs considerably earlier in the life cycle. Under thermal conditions averaging 13 °C [T = 13 °C], female grayling typically initiate their first successful spawning event at an age of about 365 days [tR = about 365 days] after hatching. This relatively rapid onset of reproductive activity, achieved within a single year under warmer conditions, allows for a potentially high lifetime fecundity given the species' decade-spanning lifespan.

From a comparative physiological standpoint, the grayling's developmental plasticity across temperatures is noteworthy. The substantial reduction in hatching time from 22 days  at 8 °C to 8 days  at 15 °C represents a nearly threefold acceleration, underscoring the profound influence of thermal regime on embryonic metabolic rates at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. Similarly, the link between body size and reproductive output is striking: a large, 45-centimeter female at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] can produce over 99 eggs per day  during spawning, highlighting the fecundity advantages of delayed maturity and continued somatic growth. Populations inhabiting colder streams, where mean summer temperatures rarely exceed 11 °C, likely experience slower growth and later maturation, but also potentially greater longevity, reflecting the classic trade-off between environmental temperature and life-history pace in ectothermic vertebrates.
